The correlation between Bleich’s financial market abuses and his litigation misconduct is 
profound and undeniable. In both arenas, the strategy relies entirely on asymmetric leverage, 
the obfuscation of material facts, and the exploitation of procedural delays to shift immense 
systemic or financial risk onto counterparties.1 In the financial markets, Bleich exploited 
Continuous Net Settlement (CNS) loopholes to avoid borrowing costs; in the judicial system, he 
exploits equitable injunctions to inflict carrying costs.1 Furthermore, Bleich’s utilization of 
offshore master-feeder structures in the Cayman Islands to avoid regulatory scrutiny aligns 
flawlessly with his evasive procedural maneuvers in civil court, such as the deliberate 
circumvention of Hague Convention service protocols.1 
When synthesized, these disparate data points confirm that the derogatory findings identified 
across Bleich’s enterprises are not isolated anomalies or clerical errors. Rather, they are the 
manifestation of a cohesive, career-spanning strategy of regulatory and judicial exploitation. 
For prospective institutional investors, limited partners, prime brokers, and judicial tribunals, the 
entities directed by Michael Bleich present substantial, and potentially unmitigable, 
reputational, operational, and counterparty risks.1 
2. Foundational Modus Operandi: Lehman Brothers, 
BATS Trading, and the Genesis of Structural 
Exploitation 
To accurately contextualize the regulatory violations and litigation misconduct that define 
Michael Bleich's later career, it is necessary to examine his foundational role within the 
institutional equities landscape during a period of massive structural transformation in the 
United States financial markets.1 Bleich’s academic foundation is deeply rooted in quantitative 
methodologies, having earned a PhD from Duke University in 1997.1 This academic pedigree 
natively funneled into the algorithmic trading sector during its most aggressive period of 
structural expansion.1 
Market Fragmentation and Regulation NMS 
During the mid-to-late 2000s, Bleich served as the Head of Liquidity Strategy for U.S. Equities 
at Lehman Brothers, a prominent global investment bank that would eventually collapse during 
the 2008 financial crisis.1 In this senior capacity, Bleich was responsible for navigating the 
rapidly fragmenting equity markets and directing Lehman's algorithmic routing, dark pool 
utilization, and electronic trading initiatives.1 
The mid-2000s marked a chaotic transition in global finance, spurred by the SEC's 
implementation of Regulation NMS (National Market System), which mandated that orders be 
routed to the venue displaying the most competitive national best bid and offer (NBBO).1 This
